screens.title: Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you’ll learn what PAM is, how the four management groups govern authentication, and why configuring PAM correctly is essential to keep systems secure while avoiding accidental lockouts. PAM relocates authentication policy from individual programs into centrally managed stacks. That means services like SSH, sudo, and login consult a service-specific file in /etc/pam. d/ and process a series of modules grouped as auth, account, password, and session. You will see how control flags such as required, requisite, sufficient, and optional change how module successes and failures combine to produce a final result. We’ll also cover two practical modules you’ll use often: pam_pwquality to enforce strong password rules, and pam_faillock to lock accounts after repeated failures. Throughout, I’ll point out common pitfalls — for example, using a network-dependent module with requisite can cause hard failures — and show safe testing and backup practices so you don’t lock yourself out. By the end you’ll be ready to audit and edit PAM stacks safely and implement robust password and locking policies for SSH and local logins.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives prepare you to manage PAM stacks confidently. First, you’ll understand the PAM architecture and processing flow: knowing the four management groups and how a service processes modules helps you reason about authentication outcomes. Second, you’ll be able to locate and read the key configuration files under /etc/pam. d/ and /etc/security/, so you can inspect what each service requires. Third, you’ll configure common modules: set up pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib for password rules, pam_faillock for account locking, and session modules like pam_systemd or pam_limits. Finally, you’ll troubleshoot real authentication failures by reading logs and the PAM stack order. Each objective focuses on practical actions you can take on a server, with safety checks to avoid locking yourself out. For example, you’ll practice making a backup of sshd’s PAM file and testing changes from a separate console. These skills matter because PAM centralizes policy: a single misconfiguration can make many services unusable, and careful change management protects both users and services.

screens.title: PAM Architecture & Processing Flow
screens.narratorSegment: PAM’s architecture is built around services consulting a sequence of module lines grouped into four management types: auth, account, password, and session. When a service requests authentication, PAM processes each type in order for that service’s configuration file. A concrete claim: the order and the control flags together determine whether authentication succeeds, fails immediately, or continues to other modules. For example, the auth stack might contain a pam_unix. so line marked required and a pam_ldap. so line marked sufficient. If pam_unix. so fails but a later sufficient module succeeds, the overall result depends on whether any required modules failed. A common misconception is to expect the first successful module to always grant access; that only happens when a module is marked sufficient and no required modules have failed earlier. Practically, knowing this lets you design resilient stacks: keep network-dependent modules as optional or sufficient rather than requisite unless you know they are always available. In this lesson you should be able to read a /etc/pam. d/ file, list the modules in each type, and explain how control flags affect the final decision. Reflect: which modules in your environment might be vulnerable to network outages, and how would you flag them to avoid global failures?

keyIdea.title: Order plus control flags
keyIdea.text: Processing order and control flags together determine the authentication outcome; misplacing flags can make a module cause immediate denial.

content.html:
Architecture
Four management groups
Auth — verifies identity (password check via pam_unix.so, pam_ldap.so).
Account — checks validity like expiration and time-of-day.
Password — handles password changes and complexity checks.
Session — sets up environment, mounts, logs session activity.
Processing Flow
A service reads its file in /etc/pam.d/, then processes each line by type. Control flags determine how each module's result is combined.
Example stack snippet
auth    required    pam_unix.so nullok
auth    sufficient  pam_ldap.so use_first_pass
In this example, pam_unix.so is required; a failure will mark the stack as failed even if pam_ldap.so later succeeds.
Common misconception
A successful sufficient module does not guarantee success if an earlier required module has failed.
Pro tip
Keep network-auth modules as optional/sufficient to avoid system-wide lockouts when network services are intermittent.
Key Takeaway
Read stacks top to bottom and inspect control flags to predict authentication outcomes.

screens.title: Auth Management Group
screens.narratorSegment: The auth management group is responsible for verifying a user’s identity, typically by prompting for credentials and checking them against a stored verifier. A clear example is pam_unix. so which authenticates against local password hashes in /etc/shadow. Another example is pam_ldap. so when authentication is delegated to a directory service. When you configure an auth line, the control flag decides how a module’s success or failure affects the stack. A concrete scenario: you might include pam_unix. so as required so local passwords are always checked, and pam_ldap. so as sufficient so LDAP users can authenticate quickly when the LDAP server is available. A common misconception is to treat auth as only password prompts; auth modules may also perform pre-auth checks like pam_faillock’s preauth mode, which should be placed before the primary auth modules to record attempts. When editing auth stacks, always keep a recovery path — for instance, a local required module or a console account that remains accessible. Practical tip: test changes from an alternate session, and remember that misplacing a requisite auth module can immediately deny all logins if that module becomes unavailable.

keyIdea.title: Auth verifies identity
keyIdea.text: Auth modules prompt and validate credentials; placement and flags determine whether failures block further processing.

content.html:
Auth — Verify identity
Common modules
  • pam_unix.so — local passwords against /etc/shadow.
  • pam_ldap.so — LDAP-based authentication for directory users.
  • pam_faillock.so (preauth) — records failures before primary auth.
Example ordering
auth    required      pam_faillock.so preauth audit deny=3 unlock_time=600
auth    required      pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth    sufficient    pam_ldap.so use_first_pass
auth    [default=die]  pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 unlock_time=600
Preauth records attempts before password checks; authfail records failures after checks.
Misconception
Placing faillock only after auth means you miss preauth logging and some failure contexts.
Pro tip
Use try_first_pass when passing an earlier password prompt to a next module to avoid double prompts.
Key Takeaway
Auth modules are the gatekeepers — design their order and flags to preserve availability and auditability.

screens.title: Account Management Group
screens.narratorSegment: The account management group checks whether an account is allowed to perform the requested operation beyond simply supplying correct credentials. These checks include account expiry, time-of-day restrictions, and whether the account is permitted to use the service. For example, pam_nologin. so prevents logins during system maintenance, and pam_unix. so can enforce account expiration attributes. A common use is to combine faillock in the account stack to enforce a lock state recorded earlier in auth. The practical contrast to auth is that account modules do not prompt for secrets; they return success or failure based on account metadata. A misconception is thinking account checks are optional for security: they are essential for policies like expiration or concurrent session limits. When editing account stacks, ensure modules that depend on prior auth state — like pam_faillock — are present so locks actually prevent access. Think about scenarios where an account is valid but restricted by time-of-day or expiration; account checks implement those policies centrally across services. Account Management Group means account modules enforce non-credential rules like expiration and maintenance-mode restrictions that determine whether a login proceeds.. In practical terms, validating account state, expiration, and access restrictions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Account — Eligibility checks
Account modules evaluate attributes like expiration, maintenance locks, and faillock state recorded earlier.
Common modules
  • pam_unix.so — account checks for local accounts.
  • pam_nologin.so — prevents login when /etc/nologin exists.
  • pam_faillock.so — consulted to enforce lockouts.
Example account entry
account required pam_faillock.so
account required pam_unix.so
Account lines ensure that previously recorded lock state blocks access even if authentication succeeded.
Misconception
Account modules are not just optional checks — they enforce system policies after identity is confirmed.
Pro tip
Place faillock in account section to ensure locks block access regardless of auth results.
Key Takeaway
Account checks enforce eligibility rules that are separate from password verification.

screens.title: Password Management Group & pam_pwquality
screens.narratorSegment: The password management group governs password changes and enforces complexity rules when users update credentials. A widely used module for this purpose is pam_pwquality. so, and older systems may use pam_cracklib. so. These modules accept arguments that directly implement policy: minlen sets a minimum length, credit arguments like dcredit, ucredit, ocredit, and lcredit require digits, uppercase, other (special), and lowercase classes respectively. The remember argument stores a history count to prevent reuse. For example, the chapter shows a robust line: set pam_pwquality. so with retry=3 minlen=12 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 reject_username enforce_for_root remember=5. That enforces a 12-character minimum with at least one of each class, disallows passwords similar to the username, applies to root, and remembers five previous passwords. A common trap is applying overly strict rules without testing user flows; always allow retries and test with passwd. Also, mixing try_first_pass or use_authtok flags changes whether the module uses a password provided earlier in the stack. After configuring, guide users through trying passwd to see rejection messages and adjust parameters if real users cannot meet the policy. Password Management Group & pam_pwquality means pam_pwquality arguments implement length, character class, username rejection, and history rules to harden password changes.. In practical terms, enforcing complexity, history, and minimum length. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: pam_pwquality arguments implement length, character class, username rejection, and history rules to harden password changes.

content.html:
Password Policy
pam_pwquality example
password required pam_pwquality.so retry=3 minlen=12 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 reject_username enforce_for_root remember=5
This enforces minimum length, at least one digit, uppercase, lowercase, and special character, prevents username-based passwords, applies to root, and remembers five previous passwords.
Arguments explained
  • minlen — minimum characters required.
  • dcredit/ucredit/ocredit/lcredit — set negative values to require that class.
  • remember — number of old passwords to prevent reuse.
  • reject_username — disallow passwords based on the username.
Misconception
Making policies too strict without testing causes frequent help desk calls; balance security and usability.
Pro tip
Use retry=3 to allow users to correct mistakes during passwd operations.
Key Takeaway
Configure pam_pwquality with realistic defaults and verify with passwd before rolling out broadly.

screens.title: Session Management Group
screens.narratorSegment: Session modules perform setup and teardown tasks around a login, such as setting environment variables, applying resource limits, mounting home directories, or registering the session with system services. Common modules include pam_systemd. so, which integrates with systemd logind, and pam_limits. so, which applies limits configured in /etc/security/limits. conf. These modules do not authenticate the user; instead they prepare the user’s runtime environment or record session activity. For example, pam_limits can enforce file descriptor or process caps for services, which matters for multi-tenant systems. A typical misconception is to neglect session modules when hardening systems; they control the runtime behavior and can prevent resource abuse or ensure accounting records. When you edit session stacks, consider dependencies such as having home mounts available or systemd being present on the system. Always test session changes by logging in and confirming environment variables, limits, and session registration behave as expected, and remember that some session failures may prevent resource cleanup if not tested properly. Session Management Group means session modules prepare environment, limits, mounts and service registration—important for runtime behavior and resource control.. In practical terms, tasks before and after login such as environment and limits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Session — Setup & teardown
Common session modules
  • pam_systemd.so — registers the session with systemd logind.
  • pam_limits.so — applies limits from /etc/security/limits.conf.
  • pam_mkhomedir.so — creates home directories on login if missing (when used).
Why session modules matter
They control environment and resource policies. Misconfigured session modules can leave accounts without correct limits or fail to register sessions for logging and accounting.
Common Pitfall
Removing pam_systemd.so on a systemd-based host can break session accounting and desktop session behavior.
Pro tip
After session edits, log in and run limits and env checks to confirm behavior applies as expected.
Key Takeaway
Session modules ensure the login is usable and accountable; treat them as part of system hardening.

screens.title: Control Flags and Their Semantics
screens.narratorSegment: Control flags shape how module results affect the final authentication decision. Start with definitions: required means the module must succeed for the overall type to succeed, but PAM will continue processing other modules so the user gets full feedback. Requisite also requires success but causes immediate failure and stops processing on failure. Sufficient causes immediate success if no prior required module has failed. Optional does not by itself determine success but can contribute to the final result. include and substack bring in other configuration files. A concrete example: marking a network-based module as requisite can cause immediate denial if the network is down; a common error. Another real-world example: combine pam_faillock. so preauth (required) before the main pam_unix. so line, and the authfail invocation after it, to both record and enforce lockouts. When reviewing stacks, simulate outcomes mentally: if a required module fails early, subsequent sufficient modules will not help. Misreading flags is a frequent source of surprise failures, so always review both the order and the flags. Ask yourself: which modules must succeed for access, and which are only helpful when present?

keyIdea.title: Flags decide control flow
keyIdea.text: Control flags dictate whether module results stop processing, cause immediate fail, or contribute to a cumulative decision.

content.html:
Control Flags
Flags and meaning
  • required — must succeed; continue processing.
  • requisite — must succeed; fail immediately on error.
  • sufficient — success may short-circuit if no required has failed.
  • optional — does not determine success by itself.
  • include / substack — include other stacks or treat as substack.
Illustrative snippet
auth required    pam_faillock.so preauth audit deny=3 unlock_time=600
auth sufficient  pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 unlock_time=600
Here faillock records preauth, unix provides the password check, and faillock enforces the lock state after auth.
Pitfall
Using requisite for a flaky network module will cause immediate denials when the network fails.
Checklist
Review flags, test in a separate session, and prefer sufficient/optional for services that may be intermittently unavailable.
Key Takeaway
Control flags are the essential operators that combine module results into a single decision; set them intentionally.

screens.title: Configuring pam_faillock for Account Locking
screens.narratorSegment: Account locking reduces brute-force risk by tracking failures and denying access after a configured number of attempts. pam_faillock is designed to be used both before and after the primary authentication checks. A recommended pattern is to add a preauth line at the start of auth to record failures before authentication, keep your primary auth module(s) next, then add an authfail invocation to record failures that occur during authentication. Additionally include pam_faillock in the account stack as required so a locked account is blocked even if authentication would otherwise succeed. The chapter provides a sample snippet for system-auth: auth required pam_faillock. so preauth audit deny=3 unlock_time=600 auth sufficient pam_unix. so... auth [default=die] pam_faillock. so authfail audit deny=3 unlock_time=600 account required pam_faillock. so. A misconception to avoid is adding faillock only in auth without the account line; the account line ensures the recorded lock prevents subsequent access. Always test by intentionally failing logins and checking faillock status with the faillock command, and keep a backup of the file before changes. Configuring pam_faillock for Account Locking means use preauth and authfail in auth and include faillock in account to both record and enforce lockouts after repeated failures.. In practical terms, add preauth and authfail, then enforce locks in account stack. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two-phase faillock
keyIdea.text: Use preauth and authfail in auth and include faillock in account to both record and enforce lockouts after repeated failures.

content.html:
pam_faillock Example
Recommended additions
# In /etc/pam.d/system-auth (or equivalent)
auth    required      pam_faillock.so preauth audit deny=3 unlock_time=600
auth    sufficient    pam_unix.so try_first_pass
auth    [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 unlock_time=600

account required      pam_faillock.so
Why this ordering works
Preauth logs attempts before verification, authfail logs failures after verification, and the account line enforces the lock based on recorded counters.
Misconception
Failing to add faillock to account leaves a recorded failure counter without enforcement in some flows.
Test step
After editing, try three failed logins and run sudo faillock --user testuser to confirm lock state before restarting services.
Key Takeaway
Record failures, enforce locks, and verify with faillock to ensure the desired protection is in place.

screens.title: Safe Editing: Backups and Testing
screens.narratorSegment: When editing PAM files you must be deliberate: a bad edit can lock out administrators and services. The simple first step is to create backups of any file you change. For example, sudo cp /etc/pam. d/sshd /etc/pam. d/sshd. bak and sudo cp /etc/pam. d/system-auth /etc/pam. d/system-auth. bak. Use a separate console or an already-logged-in session when testing configuration changes so you can recover if SSH becomes unavailable. After making edits, validate syntax visually and test with a simple password change operation or a test SSH login. If you added pam_faillock, intentionally generate failed attempts in a controlled way to verify deny and unlock_time settings, then query status with sudo faillock --user testuser and reset with sudo faillock --user testuser --reset. A common mistake is restarting sshd immediately and closing your only session — instead, keep a working root shell or physical console available until you confirm logins succeed. These safe patterns let you harden authentication policy while preserving the ability to recover from mistakes. Safe Editing: Backups and Testing means always backup pam files, test changes from an alternate console, and verify lock and password behaviors before wide deployment.. In practical terms, protect access while changing /etc/pam.d/ files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Backup and isolate tests
keyIdea.text: Always backup PAM files, test changes from an alternate console, and verify lock and password behaviors before wide deployment.

content.html:
Safe Editing Workflow
Backup commands
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/sshd /etc/pam.d/sshd.bak
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/system-auth.bak
Keep backups with timestamps when making multiple edits.
Test commands
# Check faillock status
sudo faillock --user testuser
# Reset faillock
sudo faillock --user testuser --reset
# Change password
sudo passwd testuser
Danger
Never close your only admin session until you verify the change on a separate console.
Recovery
If locked out, restore backup file from console or use single-user mode if necessary.
Key Takeaway
Backups and alternate sessions make PAM edits safe. Validate with faillock and passwd before finishing.

screens.title: Troubleshooting PAM Failures
screens.narratorSegment: When authentication fails, troubleshooting is systematic: check logs, inspect the PAM stack, and look for misused control flags or parameter problems. Start with system logs: /var/log/secure on RHEL/CentOS or /var/log/auth. log on Debian/Ubuntu, or use journalctl to capture PAM messages. Logs often show which module returned an error and which control flag applied. Next, open the relevant /etc/pam. d/ file and read lines top to bottom, noting required and requisite modules that could cause immediate denial. For password policy problems, review pam_pwquality parameters — a too-strict minlen or improper credit settings will cause passwd to reject a new password, and logs will include hints. For locking issues, verify pam_faillock lines exist both in auth and account and check the deny and unlock_time values. One common misconfiguration is using requisite for a network-reachable module: when that network service is down, logins fail instantly. Another is accidentally placing faillock lines after a sufficient module that short-circuits before lock logic runs. Keep backups and apply changes incrementally, testing after each edit to isolate failures quickly. Troubleshooting PAM Failures means use logs and stack inspection to identify which module and control flag caused a failure, then roll back or correct parameters safely.. In practical terms, logs, stack inspection, and common misconfigurations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Systematic troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Use logs and stack inspection to identify which module and control flag caused a failure, then roll back or correct parameters safely.

content.html:
Troubleshooting Steps
Check logs
RHEL/CentOS: /var/log/secure. Debian/Ubuntu: /var/log/auth.log. Or use journalctl for PAM messages and context.
Inspect stack
Open the service file in /etc/pam.d/, read lines in type order, and note control flags for potential short-circuits.
Common problems
  • Overly strict pam_pwquality parameters rejecting valid changes.
  • Using requisite on a flaky network module causing immediate failure.
  • Failing to include faillock in account stack so locks aren't enforced.
First action
Revert to backup if a recent change caused the outage, then iterate edits more slowly.
Verify
After fixes, verify with passwd, ssh tests, and faillock queries to confirm expected behavior.
Key Takeaway
Logs plus careful review of order and flags will reveal most PAM issues; revert when needed and test incrementally.

screens.title: Implementing Strict SSH Policies: Step-by-Step
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on sequence applies the chapter’s recommendations to SSH. Step one: backup the PAM files you will modify, for example sudo cp /etc/pam. d/sshd /etc/pam. d/sshd. bak and sudo cp /etc/pam. d/system-auth /etc/pam. d/system-auth. bak. Step two: configure password complexity by editing the password stack (system-auth or common-password) and set pam_pwquality with arguments such as minlen=12 and negative credits to require each character class and remember=5 to prevent reuse. Step three: add pam_faillock lines to the auth and account sections for sshd, using preauth and authfail with deny=3 and unlock_time=300. These settings lock accounts after three failed attempts for five minutes. Step four: restart sshd only after you have an alternative session open, then test by attempting weak password changes via passwd and by performing controlled failed SSH logins to trigger faillock. Use sudo faillock --user testuser to inspect counters and sudo faillock --user testuser --reset to clear them. A common pitfall is restarting sshd without a backup session. Keep a console or secondary admin connection open during testing. Implementing Strict SSH Policies: Step-by-Step means backup, set pwquality, add faillock to auth/account, restart safely, and verify with passwd and faillock commands.. In practical terms, backup, configure pam_pwquality, add faillock, restart safely, and test. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stepwise hardening
keyIdea.text: Backup, set pwquality, add faillock to auth/account, restart safely, and verify with passwd and faillock commands.

content.html:
Hands-on Steps
1. Backup
sudo cp /etc/pam.d/sshd /etc/pam.d/sshd.bak
2. Password policy
Edit system-auth or common-password to add pam_pwquality arguments.
3. Account locking
Add pam_faillock preauth/authfail and account entries with deny=3 unlock_time=300.
Example pam_pwquality line
password requisite pam_pwquality.so try_first_pass local_users_only retry=3 minlen=12 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 reject_username enforce_for_root remember=5
Example faillock snippet for sshd
# In /etc/pam.d/sshd
auth required pam_faillock.so preauth audit deny=3 unlock_time=300
# ... existing auth lines ...
auth [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=3 unlock_time=300
account required pam_faillock.so

screens.title: Validate Policy and Use faillock Commands
screens.narratorSegment: After making PAM changes, validation ensures your policy works as intended and gives you recovery tools when it does not. Use the passwd command to test password changes; try weak and strong passwords to observe pam_pwquality enforcement messages. To test account locking, perform controlled failed SSH attempts until the configured deny threshold triggers. Then check the recorded state with sudo faillock --user testuser. This will show the current count and the remaining lock time if any. To unlock a user manually after confirming administrative intent, run sudo faillock --user testuser --reset which clears the failure record. A concrete troubleshooting example: if a user reports immediate denial after entering correct credentials, inspect logs and run faillock to see if the account is locked. Remember that manual resets bypass the unlock_time timer, so use them sparingly and log your action. Always correlate faillock output with /var/log/auth. log or journalctl entries so you understand whether failures are from incorrect passwords, misconfigured modules, or service outages. Validate Policy and Use faillock Commands means use passwd and controlled ssh attempts to trigger policy, inspect faillock status for counters, and reset when administrative intervention is required.. In practical terms, verify lock counters and reset accounts when needed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify then reset
keyIdea.text: Use passwd and controlled SSH attempts to trigger policy, inspect faillock status for counters, and reset when administrative intervention is required.

content.html:
Validation & Recovery
Check faillock
sudo faillock --user testuser
# Expected output shows fail count and unlock time
Reset when necessary after verification:
sudo faillock --user testuser --reset
Test password policy
sudo passwd testuser
# Try weak passwords to see rejection messages, then set a compliant password.
Practical note
Correlate faillock output with auth logs to determine the root cause of denials.
Audit
Log manual resets and changes to maintain an audit trail for security reviews.
Key Takeaway
Verification and controlled resets keep your policy effective while preserving access when needed.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you’ll learn what PAM is, how the four management groups govern authentication, and why configuring PAM correctly is essential to keep systems secure while avoiding accidental lockouts. PAM relocates authentication policy from individual programs into centrally managed stacks. That means services like SSH, sudo, and login consult a service-specific file in /etc/pam. d/ and process a series of modules grouped as auth, account, password, and session. You will see how control flags such as required, requisite, sufficient, and optional change how module successes and failures combine to produce a final result. We’ll also cover two practical modules you’ll use often: pam_pwquality to enforce strong password rules, and pam_faillock to lock accounts after repeated failures. Throughout, I’ll point out common pitfalls — for example, using a network-dependent module with requisite can cause hard failures — and show safe testing and backup practices so you don’t lock yourself out. By the end you’ll be ready to audit and edit PAM stacks safely and implement robust password and locking policies for SSH and local logins.

These objectives prepare you to manage PAM stacks confidently. First, you’ll understand the PAM architecture and processing flow: knowing the four management groups and how a service processes modules helps you reason about authentication outcomes. Second, you’ll be able to locate and read the key configuration files under /etc/pam. d/ and /etc/security/, so you can inspect what each service requires. Third, you’ll configure common modules: set up pam_pwquality or pam_cracklib for password rules, pam_faillock for account locking, and session modules like pam_systemd or pam_limits. Finally, you’ll troubleshoot real authentication failures by reading logs and the PAM stack order. Each objective focuses on practical actions you can take on a server, with safety checks to avoid locking yourself out. For example, you’ll practice making a backup of sshd’s PAM file and testing changes from a separate console. These skills matter because PAM centralizes policy: a single misconfiguration can make many services unusable, and careful change management protects both users and services.

In addition to reading PAM stacks, you’ll practice concrete tasks that reduce risk. You’ll configure pam_pwquality with arguments like minlen, ucredit, lcredit, dcredit, and remember to enforce complexity and history. You’ll set up pam_faillock to record failures and lock accounts after a defined deny count and unlock_time. You’ll learn to place faillock lines correctly in both auth and account stacks and why the preauth and authfail modes are used. You’ll also run commands to check and reset faillock counters and test password changes with the passwd command. Each hands-on step includes a safety pattern: make a backup of the original PAM file, edit carefully, then restart sshd only after testing on a separate console. These skills matter because PAM changes can impact every login service; practicing backups and isolated tests prevents accidental outages and helps you recover quickly if something goes wrong.

PAM’s architecture is built around services consulting a sequence of module lines grouped into four management types: auth, account, password, and session. When a service requests authentication, PAM processes each type in order for that service’s configuration file. A concrete claim: the order and the control flags together determine whether authentication succeeds, fails immediately, or continues to other modules. For example, the auth stack might contain a pam_unix. so line marked required and a pam_ldap. so line marked sufficient. If pam_unix. so fails but a later sufficient module succeeds, the overall result depends on whether any required modules failed. A common misconception is to expect the first successful module to always grant access; that only happens when a module is marked sufficient and no required modules have failed earlier. Practically, knowing this lets you design resilient stacks: keep network-dependent modules as optional or sufficient rather than requisite unless you know they are always available. In this lesson you should be able to read a /etc/pam. d/ file, list the modules in each type, and explain how control flags affect the final decision. Reflect: which modules in your environment might be vulnerable to network outages, and how would you flag them to avoid global failures?

The auth management group is responsible for verifying a user’s identity, typically by prompting for credentials and checking them against a stored verifier. A clear example is pam_unix. so which authenticates against local password hashes in /etc/shadow. Another example is pam_ldap. so when authentication is delegated to a directory service. When you configure an auth line, the control flag decides how a module’s success or failure affects the stack. A concrete scenario: you might include pam_unix. so as required so local passwords are always checked, and pam_ldap. so as sufficient so LDAP users can authenticate quickly when the LDAP server is available. A common misconception is to treat auth as only password prompts; auth modules may also perform pre-auth checks like pam_faillock’s preauth mode, which should be placed before the primary auth modules to record attempts. When editing auth stacks, always keep a recovery path — for instance, a local required module or a console account that remains accessible. Practical tip: test changes from an alternate session, and remember that misplacing a requisite auth module can immediately deny all logins if that module becomes unavailable.

The account management group checks whether an account is allowed to perform the requested operation beyond simply supplying correct credentials. These checks include account expiry, time-of-day restrictions, and whether the account is permitted to use the service. For example, pam_nologin. so prevents logins during system maintenance, and pam_unix. so can enforce account expiration attributes. A common use is to combine faillock in the account stack to enforce a lock state recorded earlier in auth. The practical contrast to auth is that account modules do not prompt for secrets; they return success or failure based on account metadata. The password management group governs password changes and enforces complexity rules when users update credentials. A widely used module for this purpose is pam_pwquality. so, and older systems may use pam_cracklib. so. These modules accept arguments that directly implement policy: minlen sets a minimum length, credit arguments like dcredit, ucredit, ocredit, and lcredit require digits, uppercase, other (special), and lowercase classes respectively. The remember argument stores a history count to prevent reuse. For example, the chapter shows a robust line: set pam_pwquality. so with retry=3 minlen=12 dcredit=-1 ucredit=-1 ocredit=-1 lcredit=-1 reject_username enforce_for_root remember=5. That enforces a 12-character minimum with at least one of each class, disallows passwords similar to the username, applies to root, and remembers five previous passwords. Control flags shape how module results affect the final authentication decision. Start with definitions: required means the module must succeed for the overall type to succeed, but PAM will continue processing other modules so the user gets full feedback. Requisite also requires success but causes immediate failure and stops processing on failure. Sufficient causes immediate success if no prior required module has failed. Optional does not by itself determine success but can contribute to the final result. include and substack bring in other configuration files. A concrete example: marking a network-based module as requisite can cause immediate denial if the network is down; a common error. Another real-world example: combine pam_faillock. so preauth (required) before the main pam_unix. so line, and the authfail invocation after it, to both record and enforce lockouts. When reviewing stacks, simulate outcomes mentally: if a required module fails early, subsequent sufficient modules will not help. Misreading flags is a frequent source of surprise failures, so always review both the order and the flags. Ask yourself: which modules must succeed for access, and which are only helpful when present?

Account locking reduces brute-force risk by tracking failures and denying access after a configured number of attempts. pam_faillock is designed to be used both before and after the primary authentication checks. A recommended pattern is to add a preauth line at the start of auth to record failures before authentication, keep your primary auth module(s) next, then add an authfail invocation to record failures that occur during authentication. Additionally include pam_faillock in the account stack as required so a locked account is blocked even if authentication would otherwise succeed. Next, open the relevant /etc/pam. d/ file and read lines top to bottom, noting required and requisite modules that could cause immediate denial. For password policy problems, review pam_pwquality parameters — a too-strict minlen or improper credit settings will cause passwd to reject a new password, and logs will include hints. For locking issues, verify pam_faillock lines exist both in auth and account and check the deny and unlock_time values.
